beats.script_body: On September 11, 2001, terrorists flew two hijacked planes into the World Trade Center's Twin Towers, turning the whole complex to dust and rubble and killing nearly 3000 people. Downtown Manhattan took months to recover from the ghastly fumes wafting from the ruins, as forlorn missing-person posters grew ragged on brick walls. beats.script_body: No one shaped the physical city of the 20th century more than urban planner Robert Moses — wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system, plus endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision did away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses in favor of sweeping parks and soaring towers — and his efforts to bulldoze neighborhoods so enraged preservationists that their pushback led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.
key_claims: Robert Moses shaped the 20th-century city more than anyone
He built the Triborough Bridge, Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, West Side Hwy and Long Island parkways
Preservationist pushback against his demolitions led to the 1965 Landmarks Preservation Commission
beats.source_passage: Robert Moses, an urban planner who would influence the physical shape of the city more than anyone else in the 20th century – either wonderfully or tragically, depending on whom you ask. He was the mastermind behind the Triborough Bridge (now the Robert F Kennedy Bridge), Jones Beach State Park, the Verrazzano–Narrows Bridge, the West Side Hwy and the Long Island parkway system – not to mention endless highways, tunnels and bridges. His vision was one of doing away with intimate neighborhoods of brownstones and town houses, and of creating sweeping parks and soaring towers. The approach got preservationists fired up and their efforts to stop him from bulldozing neighborhoods led to the Landmarks Preservation Commission being formed in 1965.

beats.script_body: In 2012, superstorm Hurricane Sandy struck New York. A prestorm surge on October 28 turned parts of Brooklyn and New Jersey into a New World Venice, but Sandy saved her ultimate blow for the next day — cyclonic winds and drenching rain caused severe flooding and property damage, including to the subway system, the Hugh L Carey Tunnel and the World Trade Center site. A major power blackout plunged much of Lower Manhattan into surreal darkness, and trading at the New York Stock Exchange was suspended for two days.

Sandy caused severe flooding to the subway, Hugh L Carey Tunnel and WTC site
A blackout darkened Lower Manhattan and the NYSE suspended trading for two days

beats.script_body: The traumatic '70s — which hit bottom in 1977 with a citywide blackout and the terrorizing serial killer David Berkowitz — saw rents fall, which nourished an exciting alternative culture. Artists staged performances in abandoned schools, opened galleries in unused storefronts and revived the hair-dye industry with the punk-rock aesthetic. Ramones-loving punks turned former warehouses into pulsing meccas of nightlife, transforming the old industrial precincts of SoHo and Tribeca into America's center of tattooing and independent filmmaking.

beats.script_body: The first European to muscle in came aboard the French vessel La Dauphine, piloted by the Florentine Giovanni da Verrazzano. He explored the Upper Bay in 1524, deemed it a 'very beautiful lake,' and — while anchored off Staten Island — attempted to kidnap some of the Native Americans he encountered. His was the opening move in several decades of European raids on Lenape villages that cultivated the Lenape's deep mistrust of outsiders.

beats.script_body: After Willem Kieft let the colony fall into disrepair, Peter Stuyvesant stepped in to fix the demoralized settlement — making peace with the Lenape, establishing markets and a night watch, repairing the fort and digging a canal under what is now Canal St. His vision of an orderly trading port drew on his time as governor of Curacao, and the booming Caribbean sugar economy inspired an investment in slave trading that pushed New Amsterdam's enslaved workforce to 20 percent of the population. By the 1650s, warehouses, workshops and gabled houses were spreading back from the river's edge on Pearl St.

The burgeoning sugar economy in the Caribbean inspired an investment in slave trading that soon boosted New Amsterdam's slave workforce to 20% of the population. By the 1650s, warehouses, workshops and gabled houses were spreading back from the dense establishments at the river's edge on Pearl St.

Reporter and photographer Jacob Riis illuminated the widening gap between the classes by writing about it in the New York Tribune and in his now-classic 1890 book, How the Other Half Lives, eventually forcing the city to pass much-needed housing reforms.

The explosion of wartime activity led to a huge housing crunch that brought New York its much-imitated, tenant-protecting Rent Control Law.
